Where it began

Adam Gilchrist was born on 14 November in Bellingen, in northern New South Wales, the youngest of four, to Stan and June Gilchrist. The family moved around country towns, and when he was 13 they settled in Lismore. There he led the side at Kadina High School. In 1989 a scholarship took him to London for a year with Richmond Cricket Club.

He began his first-class career with New South Wales, but a keeping place was hard to come by there, so in 1994 he moved west to Western Australia. The Perth crowd were not sure about the newcomer at first. He soon won them round.

The player

He played 96 Tests between 1999 and 2008, scoring 5,570 runs at 47.61 with 17 hundreds and 26 fifties, and he took 379 catches and made 37 stumpings. He started as he meant to go on: 81 and six dismissals on debut at the Gabba, then 149 not out in his second Test, putting on 238 with Justin Langer to chase down 369.

In Johannesburg in 2002 he made 204 not out from 212 balls, the fastest Test double hundred at the time. At Perth in December 2006 he reached a hundred against England from 57 balls. He was the first man to hit 100 sixes in Tests, and when he stood in as captain he won four of his six Tests, including a series in India in 2004.

What made him special

His Test runs came at a rate of 82 for every hundred balls, then the third-quickest on record, and an innings from him could turn a match in a session. In one-day cricket he opened, and he made fifty or more in three World Cup finals in a row, ending with 149 against Sri Lanka in 2007, then the highest score in any World Cup final. He was also known for walking when he knew he was out, even when the umpire had not given it.

His glovework had its doubters. Some thought Darren Berry the neater keeper of the day. Gilchrist's reply was 379 Test catches and 37 stumpings, which is quite an argument.

Away from the middle

He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, won the Allan Border Medal, and is a Member of the Order of Australia. In 2007 his fellow players voted him Australia's greatest one-day cricketer. After leaving international cricket he played six IPL seasons with Deccan Chargers and Kings XI Punjab, and was the first man to reach 1,000 IPL runs. He later turned to commentary.

And finally

In his last top-class match he bowled one ball, the only one of his T20 career, and it took the wicket of Harbhajan Singh. Most bowlers would settle for a strike rate like that.
